gist: Dylan Patel (SemiAnalysis) says permitting, not labor or equipment, is pushing multiple gigawatts of US data center capacity from 2027 into 2028, while a SemiAnalysis poll shows 49% of people near 100MW data centers don't know they exist. He argues Meta's Muse and Instinct out-product OpenAI despite weaker models, reveals 45% of SemiAnalysis's $15M AI spend now goes to persistent agents via Perplexity, and discloses a $500M early-stage infrastructure fund alongside the Citrini acquisition.

themes.theme: Data center permitting and local backlash

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis has pushed multiple gigawatts of data center capacity out of 2027 into 2028, and quite a few 2028 gigawatts further out, not because of labor, equipment or construction limits but because permits are unavailable.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Permitting, not supply chain, is now the binding constraint on AI capacity timing; capex and GPU deployment schedules for 2027-28 face slippage risk.
insights.quote: we pushed back you know multiple gigawatts out of 2027 into 2028

insights.claim: Dylan Patel thinks Texas's new governor (Hinojosa) will not stop data centers outright but holds powerful levers via water, wastewater, stormwater and air permits, and a union-labor mandate is the biggest risk given very little union labor in Texas.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Texas data center pipelines (including off-grid, gas-powered sites stoppable via air permits) carry policy risk; watch the union-labor stance.

insights.claim: A SemiAnalysis poll with David Shor found 49% of people in counties with a 100MW+ data center did not know one existed in their county, and only 40% knew of a planned 100MW site coming within three years.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Anti-data-center sentiment is diffuse and narrative-driven rather than local and experiential, so it can be addressed with targeted community benefits.

insights.claim: Patel notes most jurisdictions banning data centers or running moratoriums have no meaningful data center capacity anyway, and data centers were not a top issue in election exit polls versus inflation and the war in Iran.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Headline bans overstate real capacity impact; focus on permits in jurisdictions where capacity is actually planned.

insights.claim: Patel argues data center operators could subsidize power for everyone within a 30-mile radius at negligible cost relative to project economics, defusing local opposition over electricity prices.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Community power subsidies are a cheap de-risking tool; operators that adopt them should see fewer permitting delays.

insights.claim: Patel claims all of Elon Musk's data center capacity uses about as much embedded water as three In-N-Out restaurants once the beef supply chain is counted, and a New York Times bestseller overstated data center water use by roughly 1000x.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Water-use objections to data centers are largely misinformed and well-designed sites can neutralize them.

insights.claim: Patel says data centers can fail communities when they get property tax breaks, connect to the grid and raise prices, and employ almost nobody after construction, creating a boom-bust dynamic.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Deal structures (tax abatements, grid vs. behind-the-meter power) determine local political durability of a site.

insights.claim: Patel expects space-based data centers to be a meaningful solution only later this decade, perhaps a gigawatt in space around 2030, and would take the over on Elon Musk's 2028 target, so space solves nothing for the next three to four years.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Discount near-term space-compute narratives in SpaceX-related valuations; terrestrial permitting stays the constraint.

themes.theme: AI lab competition and product quality

insights.claim: Patel says Anthropic crushed Q2, OpenAI crushed Q3 while Anthropic did 'okay', and Anthropic is now back to crushing it with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 while OpenAI keeps delaying model releases.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Lab leadership rotates quarter to quarter; avoid overindexing on single data points in pre-IPO valuations.

insights.claim: Patel argues Meta's Muse and Instinct are far better products than OpenAI's Dots despite worse underlying models, because OpenAI's safety layer (Guardian) overzealously restricts what Dots and Codex will do.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Product and harness quality, not model quality alone, determines consumer and agent share; Meta's consumer AI position may be underrated.

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis went from zero to 45% of its $15 million annual AI spend on persistent agents in a few months, mostly through Perplexity Computer (running Claude and OpenAI models underneath) rather than Anthropic's or OpenAI's own agent products.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Persistent agents are rapidly becoming a major enterprise AI spend category, and harness providers can capture spend from model labs.
insights.quote: 45% of our $15 million a year AI spend being persistent agents

insights.claim: Patel expects consumer AI products like Muse and Instinct to be sticky, coding tools like Claude Code and Codex not to be because developers switch easily, and enterprise contracts to be sticky.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Value AI coding revenue with higher churn assumptions than consumer or enterprise-contract revenue.

insights.claim: Patel has seen Anthropic offer enterprise customers discounts conditional on 70%+ of their AI spend going to Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Share-of-wallet contracts lock in enterprise revenue and squeeze competing labs within accounts.

insights.claim: Patel calls OpenAI's chat app a badly designed product for a billion-user app, with confusing model and reasoning-effort options, and says both OpenAI and Anthropic are bad at product, cycling through hired Meta VPs.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Product execution is a competitive weakness for the leading labs ahead of their IPOs.

insights.claim: Patel says Instinct primarily runs on open models yet beats OpenAI on product, and appears to have staying power with lots of users, though he is unsure it is worth its valuation.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Open models plus strong product can compete with frontier labs at the application layer.

insights.claim: Patel expects most AI startups to fail but sees ROI at fast-growing companies like Sierra and Harvey, despite possibly high customer acquisition costs.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Back vertical AI apps with clear revenue traction; expect a broad shakeout among the rest.

insights.claim: Patel questions whether inference providers justify their valuation multiples, and notes many application companies are near pure pass-throughs, citing Harvey's seesawing margins and suspecting Perplexity's margins are not high.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Gross-margin pass-through risk is the key diligence item for AI application and inference businesses.

insights.claim: Molly O'Shea notes a heavy AI IPO calendar: SpaceX (now an AI company) and Cerebras went public earlier this year, with Anthropic and OpenAI to come; Patel says markets smooth valuations more than the rotating 'top dog' narratives suggest.
insights.speaker: Molly O'Shea (host)
insights.so_what: IPO supply from AI labs will test public market appetite; narrative swings may matter less for valuations than feared.

insights.claim: Dylan Patel has raised a $500 million solo-GP early-stage venture fund focused on seed and Series A infrastructure, from robotics to silicon, optics, manufacturing and networking hardware, firewalled from SemiAnalysis research.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A well-informed hardware specialist is deploying significant early capital into AI infrastructure startups; signals where expert money sees opportunity.

insights.claim: Patel avoids application investing because he lacks expertise in scaling consumer apps, and argues hardware requires both a great founder and a great idea, unlike software where VCs back founders to figure it out.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Hardware VC diligence must weigh the technical idea heavily, favoring specialist investors.

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis acquired Citrini (captioned 'Catrini'), which turned bearish on AI months ago and remains editorially independent, while Patel stays long-term bullish on AI.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Two influential research shops under one owner hold opposing AI views; Citrini's bearish calls can move markets, as its February paper did.

insights.claim: Patel says SemiAnalysis believes some of Nvidia's practices toward certain neoclouds are anti-competitive, and publicly flags that Iris Energy has unreliable cluster technology but valuable powered land.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: For neocloud names, powered land may be the real asset; Nvidia allocation practices could draw regulatory scrutiny.

insights.claim: Patel says SemiAnalysis has publicly reported that Fluidstack's data centers are delayed even though he holds a large personal investment in the company.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Fluidstack capacity timelines may slip; independent research flagged delays despite insider ownership.

insights.claim: Patel says legacy research firms like Gartner and IDC are useless and Gartner operates 'like a racket', citing its ranking of IBM's coding agent above Cursor or Claude Code.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Traditional information services face disruption from independent, data-driven research firms.

themes.theme: Next 12 months: benchmarks and hardware acceleration

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis launched GDPX, a benchmark spanning cyber, chip design, hardware design, materials science, bio, quant and RSI, on which current models mostly perform poorly, and will test inference performance of Huawei, Amazon and AI-startup chips.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: New third-party benchmarks of non-Nvidia accelerators could shift sentiment on custom silicon competitiveness.

insights.claim: Patel predicts that within a year the number of companies building hardware, and doing it well, will skyrocket as AI accelerates hardware innovation, with particular excitement for packaging, networking and memory technologies.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Favors early-stage hardware and semiconductor-niche bets (advanced packaging, networking, memory).
